sources.source: Modern Data 101, "Data Products: A Case Against Medallion Architecture"

items.item: Not every pipeline needs all three transformation stages; forcing the pattern anyway causes unnecessary processing

at.step: Reveal: layer sprawl's cost, quoted directly

items.item: That unnecessary processing shows up concretely as added latency (data must pass through every layer before it's usable) and added storage cost (the same data copied across layers)

at.step: Reveal: layer sprawl's cost, quoted directly

items.item: Because different teams apply transformations at different stages, accountability for data quality becomes fragmented, with no single clear owner

at.step: Reveal: fragmented silver-layer accountability, quoted directly

items.item: The Silver layer specifically bears the brunt of this, becoming a named bottleneck because downstream consumers pull from aggregates built without their own input

items.item: The first predict (step 3) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that a layer's name ("Silver") is itself its quality contract; the reveal sequence states each layer's contract as a separately quoted, specific behavior rather than letting the labels carry the argument

at.step: Predict: does naming a layer "Silver" automatically give it a quality contract?

items.item: The second predict (step 7) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that more layers of refinement is unconditionally better, the same fallacy pattern as the partitioning predict in de.object-storage-query-economics; the reveal at step 8 quotes the independent critique's own named cost of forcing stages a pipeline doesn't need

at.step: Predict: does forcing every pipeline through all three stages always improve its data?

items.item: The third predict (step 9) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that ownership tracks discovery location (a bug found in Gold is Gold's problem); the reveal at steps 10-11 quotes the critique's actual claim that different teams transform data at different stages, fragmenting accountability so that discovery location and true ownership are routinely different teams

at.step: Predict: whose job is it to fix a data-quality bug that surfaces in the Gold layer?

items.item: The Silver-specific bottleneck (step 11) is kept as its own reveal, separate from the general fragmented-accountability claim (step 10), because the critique source itself treats them as two distinct, if related, points — a general problem (fragmented accountability) and a specific, named consequence of it landing hardest on one particular layer
